# ADR 0064: JWT secrets generated by Terraform must satisfy the app's Joi strength rule

- Status: Accepted — implemented (`f322972`); live-verified 2026-09-26: after the re-apply the backend booted and signed in
- Date: 2026-09-26
- Extends: [ADR 0043](0043-terraform-project-adaptation.md) (D7 has Terraform generate the four secrets with `random_password`; it set no constraint on what they contain)
- Relates to: [ADR 0057](0057-terraform-state-backend-s3-native-lock.md) (generated values sit in the state in plaintext), [ADR 0063](0063-alb-dns-externaldns-and-delegation-set.md) (repeated full `apply`/`destroy` cycles are the expected use)
- 한국어: [0064-jwt-secret-generation-joi-strength-rule.ko.md](0064-jwt-secret-generation-joi-strength-rule.ko.md)

## Context

The backend's Joi schema (`backend/app.module.ts`) refuses to boot unless `ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET` and
`REFRESH_TOKEN_SECRET` are at least 32 characters long and contain a lowercase letter, an uppercase
letter, a digit and a symbol (`[^A-Za-z0-9]`). That rule was added on 2026-09-11, after a security
review found that only the presence of a value was checked (`CLAUDE.md` > Known gaps). The same
change updated the places that hold *test* secrets — CI's dummy secrets and `.env.example` — but
nothing connected it to the place that generates the real ones.

That place is `app-infra/main.tf`. [ADR 0043](0043-terraform-project-adaptation.md) D7 has Terraform
generate the four values the Helm chart's `secrets.existingSecret` needs with `random_password`, so
no secret is typed or committed. The two token secrets were `length = 48, special = false`: 48
alphanumeric characters and no symbol. (`special = false` was written for the database password,
where a symbol can break a connection string or a shell quote; the token secrets copied it, though
they appear in neither.) D7 constrains where the values come from, not what they contain, so nothing
recorded that they had to satisfy the app's rule.

The mismatch showed on the first live run after the rule existed (2026-09-26; the earlier live
deployments, 2026-08-25–27, predate it). The stack applied cleanly, the migration Job succeeded,
and the backend pod crash-looped at boot — 8 restarts in 18 minutes — while the other three
workloads were Ready. The boot log, read by the developer with the values redacted, ended in
`Config validation error: "ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET" with value "<redacted>" fails to match the required
pattern: /^(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d)(?=.*[^A-Za-z0-9]).+$/`. The refresh secret is generated the
same way and fails the same check. The session did not read the log itself, because Joi prints the
offending value.

## Decision

### D1 — Make the generator satisfy the app's rule; do not relax the rule

Both `random_password.access_token_secret` and `random_password.refresh_token_secret` become
`special = true`, `override_special = "-_"` and `min_lower = min_upper = min_numeric = min_special = 1`,
with `length` still 48. The `min_*` values make a missing class impossible instead of merely
unlikely: with two symbols in a 64-character pool, a 48-character draw has no symbol about one time
in five (`(62/64)^48 ≈ 0.22`), so `min_special = 1` is not optional. `-_` needs no escaping in a
URL, a shell or YAML, and the rule asks for one symbol, so a wider set would add risk without adding
anything the rule checks.

### D2 — The database password is left alone

`random_password.db` keeps `special = false`. Its reason (a connection string or a shell quote) still
holds, and the app has no strength rule for it beyond being present.

### D3 — Roll it out on the live stack without a chart or image change

Re-apply `app-infra/`, which replaces both `random_password` resources and the secret version;
annotate the `ExternalSecret` with `force-sync` so External Secrets copies the new value at once
(its refresh interval is 1 h); restart the backend Deployment so the pod reads the changed `Secret`.

## Alternatives rejected

Each entry says what the alternative did better, since that is the trade-off accepted. The developer
chose between three, from a comparison table.

- **Relax the Joi rule** (drop the symbol requirement). Nothing to re-apply, and it treats the rule
  as the thing that was wrong. Not chosen: it undoes a security decision made two weeks earlier
  because deploying it was inconvenient (Never Do Group 3, which wins over convenience), it edits
  `app.module.ts` (a high-blast-radius file), and it needs an image rebuild and a merge to `main`
  before it can deploy. It stays open as its own decision: a 48-character random alphanumeric secret
  carries about 285 bits, so a character-class rule is a proxy meant for human-chosen secrets, and
  replacing it with a length or entropy rule for generated ones would be a policy change with its own
  ADR, not a deployment fix.
- **Replace the value in Secrets Manager by hand** (`put-secret-value`). The fastest, with no code
  change. Not chosen: the generator stays broken, so every later apply — full apply/destroy cycles
  are the expected use ([ADR 0063](0063-alb-dns-externaldns-and-delegation-set.md)) — produces a
  secret the app refuses; the hand-set value drifts from the state; and the secret passes through the
  developer's shell.

## Consequences

- **Checked before the apply:** `terraform fmt -check` and `terraform validate` pass. The rule's
  regex, run on a sample built from the worst case the new generator allows (one character of each
  class, the rest lowercase), passes; run on the old shape (48 alphanumerics), it fails, which
  reproduces the live error.
- **Observed live (2026-09-26; the developer ran every command, the session read AWS and the cluster
  read-only):** the `app-infra/` plan said `3 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy`. The session had
  predicted `2 to add / 1 to change / 2 to destroy`, on the expectation that the secret version would
  update in place; that was wrong. The third replaced resource is inferred to be
  `aws_secretsmanager_secret_version.app` (the plan lines were not shown to the session): Secrets
  Manager shows a new `AWSCURRENT` version created at 16:06Z with the earlier one demoted to
  `AWSPREVIOUS`, while the RDS instance, ACM certificate, IAM role and S3 bucket kept their
  creation times and the Route53 zone kept its id. After `force-sync` and a restart the backend was
  `1/1 Running` with `/health/live` and `/health/ready` answering `200`, and `POST /auth/signin`
  returned an access token (179 characters, the JWT prefix `eyJ`), so the app boots and signs with
  the new secrets.
- **Accepted:** rotating the secrets invalidates any token issued under the old ones; none existed,
  because the backend had never booted. The old values remain in the state bucket's earlier versions
  in plaintext ([ADR 0057](0057-terraform-state-backend-s3-native-lock.md)) and in Secrets
  Manager's previous version until the secret is deleted (a teardown deletes it at once,
  `recovery_window_in_days = 0`).
- **Not closed:** nothing ties the generator to the Joi rule automatically, so tightening the rule
  again would fail the same way at the next live boot. A CI check would be new tooling and is not
  added here (Scope Discipline); the comment above the two resources in `app-infra/main.tf` names
  the rule, so someone editing the generator sees the constraint.
